Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Sierra Leonean mourns Ghana’s late Prof. Fred Binka, pioneering malaria researcher Source : Prof. Osman A. Sankoh 18 November 2026 11:41am Prof Fred Newton Binka ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The passing of Prof. Fred N. Binka in Ghana on 15 November 2026, at the age of 73, was a great loss to African science and to all of us who had the privilege of knowing and working with him. Fred was an outstanding scientist, a visionary leader and a generous mentor. For me, he was also a dear friend and one of the two men who greatly influenced the direction of my professional life.
I first met Fred in 2000 at a workshop in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, where scientists had gathered to discuss the demographic dynamics of populations in Africa and Asia using data from Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS) sites. At the time, I was a research scientist at the University of Heidelberg Medical School in Germany, working in the Department of Tropical Hygiene, Section of Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Public Health.
It was at that meeting that Ghanaian Fred Binka and Senegalese Dr Cheikh Mbacké, then with the Rockefeller Foundation, decided that they needed to “snatch me (Sierra Leonean) from Germany and take me to Africa.” They believed I could contribute to the development of the newly established INDEPTH Network, which was still finding its feet.
Cheikh subsequently offered me a consultancy to support Fred and the Network. I was also appointed Editor-in-Chief of INDEPTH’s first major book, Population and Health in Developing Countries , published by the International Development Research Centre (IDRC), Canada, in 2002.
In 2002, I left Germany and joined INDEPTH in Accra, Ghana, as its first Scientific Communications and External Relations Director. Fred was then the Executive Director. In 2006, I was appointed Deputy Executive Director, and in 2007, I had the privilege of succeeding him as Executive Director, a position I held until March 2018.
The circumstances surrounding my appointment remain among my fondest memories of Fred. At an Annual General Meeting, he announced that he was moving on and that the Network should begin searching for his successor. When I asked whether I could apply, he simply told me that the decision was mine. However, after I submitted my application, he organised a mock interview to help me prepare. When the actual interviews took place in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, Fred deliberately stayed away to avoid influencing the selection process.
That was Fred Binka. He believed in preparing others to lead, and he had the confidence to step aside when the time came.
Our professional relationship grew even stronger after I succeeded him. With a grant of US$17 million from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, we established the Malaria Clinical Trials Alliance (MCTA), with Fred serving as Principal Investigator. By then, he had moved to the University of Ghana as Dean of its School of Public Health, where he also encouraged me to pursue a lecturer position.
I established the MCTA Scientific Advisory Board, chaired by Dr Pascoal Mocumbi, former Prime Minister of Mozambique. Together, we worked to strengthen Africa’s capacity to conduct high-quality malaria clinical trials.
Our collaboration continued through the INDEPTH Effectiveness and Safety Studies (INESS), supported by another grant of approximately US$28.6 million from the Gates Foundation. Dr Hassan Mshinda of Tanzania, then Director of the Ifakara Health Institute, led INESS. The programme strengthened African capacity to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of malaria interventions under real-life conditions, contributing to the broader scientific effort surrounding interventions such as the RTS malaria vaccine, now used in Sierra Leone and other African countries.

Another important chapter in our collaboration was the development of the Comprehensive Health and Epidemiological Surveillance System (CHESS). INDEPTH had built considerable expertise in monitoring births, deaths, migration and causes of death. However, we recognised the need to go further by linking community-level information with health-facility data to better understand morbidity, healthcare utilisation and disease outcomes.
I secured funding from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida) to advance this work and once again invited Fred to provide scientific leadership. He readily agreed.
Years later, during my tenure as Statistician-General and CEO of Statistics Sierra Leone, we secured a 5-year $30 million World Bank funding to strengthen the statistical landscape of Sierra Leone, and also establish two CHESS sites in Pujehun and Karene Districts. It gave me particular satisfaction to see an initiative we had developed through INDEPTH finding practical expression in my own country.
One quality I admired greatly about Fred was his humility. Here was a man who had been my boss, yet he repeatedly accepted responsibilities as Principal Investigator on projects I had helped develop and secure funding for. He never allowed titles or positions to interfere with our shared scientific objectives.
He understood that leadership was not about holding on to authority but about building institutions and developing people who could carry the work forward.
Fred’s contributions to African public health were immense. His pioneering work at the Navrongo Health Research Centre in Northern Ghana, particularly in malaria research and community-based health interventions, helped demonstrate the value of rigorous population evidence. His leadership of INDEPTH strengthened scientific collaboration across Africa and Asia, while his subsequent work contributed to the development of African research capacity in clinical trials, epidemiology and health systems research.

When I think about my journey from the village of Warima, Sierra Leone, to Heidelberg and then to Accra, I remain grateful that Fred and Cheikh saw possibilities in me that I had not fully imagined for myself. Their decision in Ouagadougou in 2000 opened a new chapter in my life, and Fred remained an important part of that journey for many years.
To his family, friends, students and colleagues, I extend my deepest condolences. We have lost a remarkable African scientist whose contributions will continue to benefit generations.
Fred, you and Cheikh wanted to snatch me from Germany and bring me back to Africa. You succeeded! You gave me an opportunity, helped prepare me for leadership and continued to support me long after I succeeded you. I hope that, in my own work and in the opportunities I create for others, I have honoured the confidence you placed in me.
Your life reminds us that the true measure of leadership is not simply what we accomplish ourselves, but what we make possible for others.
Rest peacefully, Professor Fred N. Binka. Your scientific legacy endures, and your friendship and mentorship will always remain part of my life’s story.
In our circles, I was known to you as Prof. Sankoh, OS, Osman, Mallam O.
The author is Prof. Osman A. Sankoh, COR Executive Director, Centre for Health Research and Training (CHaRT-SL) University of Management and Technology (UNIMTECH) Freetown, Sierra Leone.
